takeaways: If help appears on several pages, it is in the same place relative to the other content each time: human contact details, a contact form or chat, a self-help page like an FAQ, or a chatbot.
New in WCAG 2.2, Level A. It does not require you to offer help. It requires the help you offer to be easy to find again.
People who need help are often already struggling. If the chat button moves between pages, they may never find it.
“Same relative order” is about order among the page content, not identical pixels. Users who move help themselves are fine.
failures: A contact link in the header on some pages and the footer on others
A chat button that appears in a different corner in checkout
check: Line up every template at the same screen size and mark where each help item sits.
Check the order of help items is the same relative to the header, main content and footer.
Check special templates, like checkout and account pages, that are often built separately.

quiz.question: On product pages a “Contact us” link sits in the header. On checkout pages the header is stripped down and the link moves to the footer. Does this fail 3.2.6?
options: No. Checkout is a different section, so it can differ
Yes. The help link is in a different place relative to the rest of the page
No. The rule only applies to live chat
quiz.why: A set of pages includes checkout. The help mechanism has to keep its relative position. Keep the link in the slim header too, or put it in the footer everywhere.

spec: List the help mechanisms offered and their fixed position in each layout.
Show how each help item appears in minimal templates like checkout.
Note any user setting that lets people move or hide help.
review: Where is help on this page, and is it in the same place on the others?
Did the checkout or sign-in template drop or move it?
If I were stuck, could I find help without looking?
tradeoff: Focused flows like checkout often strip the header to reduce distraction. Keep the help item in the same spot, even in a slim header. It is one link and it costs little attention.
system: Put help links and the chat launcher in the shared header and footer components, with their position locked across templates.
pitch: People who are stuck look for help where they last saw it. If it moves, they leave or call us.
